body: A man comes off watch at four in the morning somewhere in the Indian Ocean and there is no signal, and there will not be one for another three days. He sits on the steps by the funnel with a mug of instant coffee going cold in the wind, and plays a song off his phone that he downloaded in port a fortnight ago, and sings the second verse under his breath because the man he shares a cabin with is asleep and has the six o’clock. His daughter turned nine in March. He watched it on video eleven days late, on a connection that kept freezing her face at odd moments, and he has watched it several times since.

Nobody is going to build a church for that man. There is no way to. The congregation he belongs to is somewhere behind him at about eighteen knots, and whatever reaches him at four in the morning has to be something that travels.

There are Filipino workers in almost every country in the world, and the pattern is consistent wherever they turn up: in care work, in shipping, in hospitals and in other people’s households, frequently on contracts that keep them from their own families for years, and sending money home that whole towns are built on.

It is worth taking the word travel literally, because it separates the things that survive a departure from the things that do not. A congregation does not travel. It cannot: it needs a room, a rota, a fixed hour, and enough people in one place at that hour to make the hour worth keeping. Take any one of those away and it stops. That is not a weakness — it is what makes a parish a parish — but it does mean the local church is, by construction, the least portable thing the faith has. What travels is smaller and harder to confiscate. A tune. A prayer said the same way every night. A habit of nine days of something before a feast. The order in which your mother did things on a particular evening in December. None of that needs a room. It goes through customs undeclared and it fits in a phone.

This dial carries 40 international stations in 29 languages, hosted in those languages rather than translated into them afterwards. One of them is HM 339.90 — Pilipinas Inspire, in Tagalog, anchored in Manila with relays in Los Angeles and Las Vegas, and it is on air today.

The frequency was assigned knowing the audience would never be in one place, which is an odd thing to build for and an expensive one. A number on this band belongs to one station permanently and cannot be recycled, and this one has been given to listeners scattered across every time zone there is, most of whom will hear it alone, at hours no scheduler would choose. Filipino workers are in nearly every country on earth, and a great many of them spend Christmas on somebody else’s schedule. A station is one of the very few things that can be in all those places at once.

The shape of that diaspora is what makes it easy to overlook. It is not a neighbourhood you could drive to. There are cities with real Filipino communities and good churches in them — but the characteristic experience is not the community, it is the individual: one person from home in the building, in a household on a hill outside a city, on a ship, on a ward, on a night rota. Dispersed and enormous at once, and dispersion of that kind defeats almost every tool the Church has, because all of them assume that if you gather people they will be near enough to gather.

Which is why what actually carries, carries in the form of music and devotional habit rather than institution. Not because Filipino Christianity is thin on doctrine — it is not — but because habit is the part that fits in a suitcase. The dawn services in the run-up to Christmas, kept for generations at an hour that only makes sense if everybody is walking to the same building, get kept anyway by somebody walking nowhere, on a laptop, at whatever hour corresponds. The novena survives the move because it is nine days and a set of words and needs nobody’s permission. The song survives because it was already in her head before she got on the plane.
Faith that has to travel eventually finds out which parts of it were luggage and which parts were load-bearing.

The diaspora congregation deserves proper credit before anything is said about its limits, because at its best it is one of the finest things in world Christianity — a hall borrowed on a Sunday afternoon, food afterwards that takes four hours, people who will find you a job and a room and a lawyer. Nobody who has been inside one would trade it for a broadcast. But look at who is missing from that hall. The carer whose day off is Wednesday. The nurse six weeks into nights. The seafarer, obviously. The woman two buses from the nearest Filipino church, who works the hours she is told to. The hall meets when it meets, and the people whose schedules are owned by somebody else are exactly the people it cannot accommodate.
A congregation gathers. A frequency arrives.

It is Christmas morning and a woman is getting an elderly man out of bed in a house that is not hers, in a country she has been in for four years. She does his feet first, because of the circulation. She gets him into the blue jumper his daughter sent, gives him his tablets in the order they go, and puts the porridge on. The house is silent apart from the boiler. She props her phone on the arm of his chair and puts on a station from home, quietly, because it is easier than not. He listens to the whole song, then asks her what language that is, and she tells him, and he says it sounds like a hymn he used to know, and she says yes, a bit. It is the longest conversation she has had about home in eleven days. She will ring her mother at nine tonight, which is five in the morning in Manila, because that is the window they have.

Nothing in that morning was arranged by anybody. She did not choose the song, she chose the frequency, and the frequency did the rest — which is the one thing a broadcast can do that a playlist cannot, because a playlist would have handed her back what she already knew.

The limits should be stated flatly. A station cannot give her a day off, cannot visit her, cannot bring her communion, and cannot stand next to her at the funeral she will not be able to fly home for. It will not learn her name. It cannot do the four-hour meal after the service, which is honestly the part she misses most. And its figures will always look small next to the mainstream stretch of the band, because a scattered audience produces small numbers everywhere and large numbers nowhere.

That last point is not a weakness in the station. It is the reason for it. A frequency serving a scattered people will always look under-attended, because attendance is a measure built for rooms and the whole situation here is that there is no room. The right question is not how many are listening but how many places it reaches at once, and by that measure this is one of the busiest numbers on the dial — a household in the Gulf, a ward in the north of England, a ship, a night bus, a flat in Milan with the light off, all inside the same three minutes.

So this frequency is more useful than its figures will ever suggest. It is not serving a community in a place. It is serving a scattered one, at every hour, in the gaps between other people’s shifts — and it is one of the few forms of ministry that works better the more dispersed its people become, which is the opposite of everything else the Church has.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing.

The dial carries four kinds of programming — music, which is most of the band; teaching and prayer; family programming; and the international stations. The Tagalog corner is not finished: Jubilee Prayers in Tagalog holds HM 359.50, assigned, in build, not yet on air. The music station is up, though.

Put on HM 339.90 — Pilipinas Inspire. It is on air now. Tagalog praise, OPM gospel and Spirit-filled Filipino worship, anchored in Manila with relays into Los Angeles and Las Vegas so it lands on the mainland at a usable hour. Its schedule is published: Umagang Papuri in the morning, Gabing Pagsamba in the evening, both on Manila time — which means somebody working nights in Europe gets morning praise at the end of a shift, and that is not a defect, it is the whole use of a fixed clock. Send it to the person you know who is working through a holiday this year. If that person is you, put it on in whatever room you are being paid to be in, quietly, and let it run.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, which matters more here than almost anywhere, because the people this station is for are on borrowed wifi, prepaid data and hardware that has to last. Add the page to your home screen if you like. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band learns which languages and which hours people are actually reaching for, which is how the prayer station in Tagalog gets its opening date.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not evaluate it — put HM 339.90 on at an hour that suits somebody else for once, and let it play. And if you have a Filipino colleague on the ward or the site or the night desk, send them the frequency without a message attached, because it does not need one. What travels is the thing you can pass to somebody in ten seconds and that still works when they are alone at four in the morning in a time zone where nobody who loves them is awake.
